title: Automated prostate-extension grading shows a sensitivity–specificity tradeoff against pathology
summary: A cascaded segmentation and random-forest pipeline was evaluated against surgical pathology in a retrospective prostate-cancer cohort. In 127 held-out patients, one threshold produced lower sensitivity but higher specificity than the radiologist comparison. This is a bounded clinical-validation finding, without established superiority, improved surgical decisions or independent replication of the reused segmentation model.
ai_technology: Reused 3D U-Net/residual segmentation pipeline with random-forest extraprostatic-extension grading
organization: National Cancer Institute; National Institutes of Health

evidence.tested: The source split 634 prostatectomy patients into 507 development and 127 test patients. Fixed segmentation models produced prostate/lesion masks; geometric features trained random forests with repeated cross-validation. At EPE≥1, test sensitivity/specificity were 0.67/0.73 versus 0.81/0.62 for the radiologist, using pathology as reference. Four-grade balanced accuracy was limited, and individual grade AUCs ranged 0.55–0.70.
evidence.unknown: This retrospective analysis used prospectively recorded radiologist assessments, without prospective AI-model locking. Development grades partly incorporated pathology, while comparison grades came from the radiologist. Reused segmentation models and overlapping institutional recruitment periods mean the full pipeline is not established as wholly unfamiliar with test patients. No paired clinical reader-assistance or treatment-benefit trial was performed, and no general superiority is claimed.
evidence.ai_role: Learned segmentation extracted lesion/capsule features and a trained random forest mapped them to extension grades; comparison with actual surgical pathology supplies the distinct clinical-validation result. This extends a previously developed segmentation workflow rather than constituting independent replication of it.

source_review.scope: Read actual primary clinical selection/patient split, radiologist/pathology label construction, fixed segmentation-feature and random-forest training/evaluation Methods, pathology-reference test Results and comparison limits. Source reference27 checked against previously read segmentation paper. Individual overlap across reused model training and this cohort not reconstructed.
